story.title: Pope Leo XIV Warns AI Could Undermine Humanity During France Visit
story.summary: Pope Leo XIV expressed concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence, describing it as a potential 'paradise of machines' that could undermine humanity. He raised fundamental questions regarding human existence in the context of technological advancement, nuclear threats, and other existential risks during his visit to France.

explore_lenses.label: Why is AI central to Leo’s France visit?
explore_lenses.title: A planned forum on technology and human dignity
explore_lenses.summary: The warning fits a broader Vatican campaign to frame AI as a question of human dignity and public responsibility, not only innovation. France’s UNESCO stop gives the message an international policy audience.

claims.text: The Vatican’s official itinerary scheduled Pope Leo XIV to visit UNESCO in Paris on September 25 during his September 25–28 France trip.

UNESCO said its September 25 program with Leo would address AI, information integrity, education and artistic creation, and would bring together young people, artists, researchers and decision-makers.
Leo’s stated perspective is that technological decisions must be joined to conscience and responsibility, and that people must not be reduced to productivity, cognitive performance or data.

points: The Vatican’s official itinerary scheduled Pope Leo XIV to visit UNESCO in Paris on September 25 during his September 25–28 France trip.

UNESCO said its September 25 program with Leo would address AI, information integrity, education and artistic creation, and would bring together young people, artists, researchers and decision-makers.
Leo’s stated perspective is that technological decisions must be joined to conscience and responsibility, and that people must not be reduced to productivity, cognitive performance or data.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The official Vatican text for the September 25 France remarks was not yet available in the sources consulted, so the precise setting and full wording of the reported “paradise of machines” phrase cannot be independently assessed here.
explore_lenses.note: Researched context; forecasts and viewpoints are labeled and attributed.

explore_lenses.label: What harms does Leo associate with AI?
explore_lenses.title: Control, discrimination and human dependence
explore_lenses.summary: Leo’s concern is not that all AI is inherently harmful; he has paired recognition of possible benefits with warnings about systems that replace human judgment or concentrate power without safeguards.

claims.text: In a September 24 address, Leo said AI can be used for surveillance, manipulation and discrimination, while also noting that its overall effects remain uncertain and that it can offer grounds for hope.

Leo has warned that the pace of AI development raises the question of whether machines can be controlled and whether humanity could become a victim of its inventions; he singled out delegating decisions about human life to machines as a serious problem.
His 2026 encyclical identifies material as well as social stakes: more complex AI systems require computing, storage, data centers and energy-intensive infrastructure.

explore_lenses.label: What happens after the opening warning?
explore_lenses.title: The trip broadens from AI to peace and society
explore_lenses.summary: The warning is the opening of a four-day program rather than a stand-alone AI announcement. The remaining itinerary is designed to connect technology with youth, social support, the French church and European peace.

claims.text: After the UNESCO visit, the published September 25 program included vespers at Notre-Dame and a youth prayer vigil at Stade de France; subsequent stops included a social-support center, Lourdes and Metz.
Holy See spokesman Matteo Bruni said the trip would focus on faith, culture and Europe, with an encounter in Metz centered on Europe, peace and unity.

UNESCO’s stated aim was a reflection on AI, education and peace, indicating that the immediate next step is dialogue among policymakers, researchers, cultural figures and young participants rather than a new binding international AI rule.

story_report.summary: Pope Leo XIV used his first papal visit to France to warn that artificial intelligence could threaten humanity and to raise wider questions about human existence amid technological and nuclear risks. His Sept. 25 program included a UNESCO event on AI, information integrity, education and artistic creation, bringing young people, artists, researchers and decision-makers into the discussion. The immediate outcome identified in official materials was dialogue on AI, education and peace, not a new international rule or commitment.

sections.heading: Leo’s AI Ethics Framework
sections.body: The pope has argued that technological choices must be guided by conscience and responsibility, rather than treating people as measures of productivity, cognitive performance or data. In other 2026 statements, he said AI can enable surveillance, manipulation and discrimination, while acknowledging that its effects remain uncertain and may also offer grounds for hope. He has also questioned whether humans can retain control of machines and opposed delegating decisions about human life to them.

sections.heading: AI’s Social and Material Stakes
sections.body: Leo’s published assessment extends beyond the immediate uses of AI to the infrastructure supporting it. His 2026 encyclical says increasingly complex systems require computing capacity, storage, data centers and energy-intensive infrastructure. These are ethical assessments and stated concerns, however, not evidence that a particular AI system will necessarily cause the harms he describes.

sections.heading: France Visit Continues Beyond UNESCO
sections.body: After the UNESCO visit, the published Sept. 25 schedule included vespers at Notre-Dame and a youth prayer vigil at Stade de France. The remainder of the Sept. 25–28 trip included visits to a social-support center, Lourdes and Metz. Holy See spokesman Matteo Bruni said the visit would focus on faith, culture and Europe, with the Metz encounter addressing Europe, peace and unity.

related_stories.title: Shooting Victim from 2024 Trump Rally in Butler Passes Away
related_stories.summary: James Copenhaver, 76, who was shot during an assassination attempt at a Trump campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died from complications related to his injuries. The shooting also resulted in the death of another individual and grazed Trump's ear with a bullet. Trump expressed his condolences, calling Copenhaver's death a 'tremendous loss.'
